en: First Canto:

May the feet of Śrīkaṇṭha’s beloved, which delight the virtuous and are anointed by the luster of her moon-like nails, shine as if smiling with the unbroken, towering tail-hair of the sacrificial horse. 1.1ab–cd.
May that auspicious foot of yours be for our prosperity— the foot which, stained with blood in battle,
the gods themselves, bowing down together, washed not with water but with the very tears of their joy.
Even the half-chewed pieces of meat from the battlefield, clinging between his teeth—
May Bhadrakālī, who is said to draw forth auspicious things with the tip of her little finger, bring you prosperity.

May the face of Rati, which Girijā approached as she gazed upon it— smiling because the ancient cities were bowing before her enemy due to the offense of the blazing fish-bannered god— be for our delight.
May she be auspicious for you— she by whom the Lord of the Mountains (Śiva), heavy with the glance of her intentional look,
still to this day does not digest the fierce, transforming, and singular-arrowed god of love within him.
May Sarasvatī, whose lute rests upon the lotus-hand of the Goddess of Speech, delight you as she resonates with melody.
Since she, like a flowing wave of nectar for the ears, takes up residence upon the tongues of poets;
may the Daughter of the Creator, the mother of the three worlds, bestow blessings throughout the triple world.
For it is as if by serving her two lotus feet that the Fish-Haṃsa attained the state of a poet.
Whose form was manifested from milk, who is the sister of nectar and is united with the consumer of honey (the sun), and who,
as if perfumed by lotuses, is alluring to the worlds— we praise her.
He upon whom the path of the Vedas, which destroys the afflictions of rebirth, rests.
I am born for this certain Supreme Lord, who has become the object of my heart and eyes.
I bow to that Grandfather (Brahmā), the lord of the mountain of the rivers of the Vedas,
who, having created the Goddess of Speech— the mother of the world— attained the status of her maternal grandfather.
I pay homage to that foremost of the forbearing, the sole lord of the universe,
who bears upon his head the moon— the maker of night— even as it touches him with its crooked rays and its feet.
May the river of Śiva’s head protect you— he who, assuming a slender form in his presence, appears like the enemy of Smara (Kāma).
The moon, with its rays turned upward, seems to perform austerities out of grief for its friend, the flower-armed god of love.
Though he has Ugra as his father, Caṇḍī as his wife, Agnibhū as his son, and the double-tongued serpents dwelling nearby—
may that one supreme cause of the world’s welfare protect us, despite being of such a nature.
I ever salute that singular body of Śiva and Śivā, which, under the pretext of the jar-like breasts on its left side,
became the self-born hero Manobhū (the Mind-born God) who attained death in battle in the form of a *liṅga*.
Thinking, "Let this one alone be the creator (*dhātṛ*) of those who fall here," he was resorted to by his husband as he fell.
May that Hari, who is like a lion to the lordly elephant-demons blinded by intoxication, ever grant you joy.
May that Boar bring you delight, who performed his sport in the ocean that reached only to his forefeet;
he who recognized the earth clinging to his tusk through the sounds of the hymns of praise offered by her.

May that Puṃskesarī protect you— he from whom the elephant-faced [Ganeśa], though his pride had constantly turned away from him out of fear even at the mere scent of him, now approaches the gods with joy for the sake of praising him. May he protect you, who under the pretext of massaging the limbs of [Kṛṣṇa] weary from the burden of Mount Govardhana— 1.17ab–1.18ab
Afflicted by love, the gopīs obtained the pleasure of an embrace without hesitation even in the presence of their elders.

(1.18cd) "O Rādhā, that lower lip which was offered by your beloved for the sake of success in the struggle of passion—give it back to him! For she has a desire to receive this gift from even your Lord, the Wielder of the Discus. (1.19)

May there be prosperity for you through Rāma, who, with his sword as a ladle, offered the kingdom of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa as fragrant clarified butter into the fire of his own valor, kindled by fuel of *palāśa* wood. I pay homage to the daughter of the Lord of Videha, whose fame for the narrative of her abandonment...

That eulogy of the glory of the noble Rāma, though beloved by the whole world, becomes an object of displeasure [to her]. (1.21cd) "May Rāma, who broke the formidable bow and did a favor for Janaka, be my husband, and not Rāvaṇa"—how is it that Gaurī, whom her father constantly entreated in this way, is not Maithilī among women? (1.22ab–1.22cd)
May that tusk of Lambodara, possessing a splendor like that of the moon’s brother (the elephant Airāvata), be for the abundance of your contentment—
(1.23ab) That tusk which, stationed near the river of rut, destroys the luster of the white umbrella (of Indra)—
(1.23cd) May it be worshipped by you all, as it repeatedly shakes the head of the many-faced one (Gaṇeśa). (1.24ab)
May that courtyard of the fierce-rayed Sun—the gateway to the city of the enemy of the Daityas—cut through my sorrow; it is as if it beckons success every day to those who love prostrating before it.
There, a mass of rays shines like a row of sprouts, appearing like a garland for the archway.
With devotion I salute the moon, who possesses eighty rays and bestows a new body upon those who are bodiless;

he who, having caused the destruction of darkness, adorns the faces of the quarters with the cessation of delusion. Even the hero Smara, though his retinue consists of cowards, is worthy of worship because of him [the moon], from whose very ashes his own limbs were reduced to ash.
I suspect that even now the Moon-crested Lord, filled with apprehension, does not abandon his refuge in Durgā.
Salutations to those three Vedas, who bear the sons of Śreyas born from another;
indeed, this assembly of great sages assumes the role of a protector for that child.
Victorious are those many [faces] of whom there is but one face, which is the cause of the three worlds.
Victorious also is he whose form is inconceivable, yet who possesses many faces for that single one.
I bow to him, that master of the scriptures, who is like the preeminent [face] among sages, [the preeminent one] among poets.

The image of Rāghava’s glory was installed as the presiding deity in his own temple of poetry. I praise that son of Satyavatī, whose work— being the secret of the *Ṛgveda*, the transformation of the *Yajurveda*, the essence of the *Sāmaveda*, and the foremost among the venerable— satisfies the three worlds.

I bow to the *Rāmāyaṇa*, which—like the *Mahābhārata*—has the son of the Wind-god as its radiant hero, in which Droṇa is brought low and the King of Sindhu is cast out, and which, through the deeds of Rāma, steals away the lineage of the monkeys.
(1.32) I bow to him who, by his very use of the vernacular, brought about the lack of prestige for great poets regarding the divine language. (1.33ab)
Who would not consider the *Bṛhatkathā* of this Guṇāḍhya to be truly great?
(1.33cd) Truly, by virtue of their mastery of the aesthetic essence of literature (*sāhityarasa*), Subandhu and other preeminent poets have attained perfection;
for even when they are invisible, their speech is heard directly, bringing delight to the ear. (1.34ab–1.34cd)
Having reflected upon the words of the illustrious Kālidāsa, my mind finds no delight in the poetry of others.
Alas, would a swarm of bees ever abandon the *pārijāta* tree to find joy in the *sindhuvāra*?
I suspect that for a long time Māgha, Murāri, and the other great poets shall remain well-established in the presence of the Creator.
By whom streams of honey and milk have been set flowing in the world under the guise of their own power of speech;
who constantly worship Sarasvatī and do not even accept the wealth of others;
and who possess riches through livelihoods cultivated by self-restraint—what purer thing could there be than these poets? (1.36cd–1.37)

Worthy poets are not made venerable by their age, but by the canopies of their poetry which prioritize aesthetic flavor (rasa). Jewels become worthy of honor due to their exceptional brilliance, not like stones because of their bulk.
One who claims another’s poem as his own is recognized here by the wise as a thief of poetry.
Having seen this [work] in the hands of an unworthy person, who indeed would believe that it is his?
(1.39cd) What benefit is there for the author by composing poetry with the subject matter provided by others?
(1.40ab) For as long as he lives, he has cause for apprehension regarding those learned in the scriptures; and once he has perished, he gains no fame here. (1.40cd)
Let that Sarasvatī of the preeminent poets, whose flow is unimpeded, be saluted—she who, like the twilight not yet attained, cannot indeed be entered by wicked cranes;
she who, resting upon aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and beautiful through her artful turns (*vakratā*), reveals a brilliance like that of refined gold. (1.41–1.42ab)
The eloquent utterance of only a certain poet shines upon his face, like the fang of the Lord of Elephants.

(1.42cd) Is even that essence of poetry worthy of praise which, when drunk by the cupped hands of the ears, does not quickly manifest a transformation of the listener’s body through tears of joy and trembling of the head? (1.43)
Victorious are those clouds of the virtuous, who exert themselves for the joy of all;
by them, a supreme burning is produced in the bodies of the wicked, as if they were blades of *yavāsa* grass.
When the fire of suffering has begun to blaze within those whose souls are distressed, by the wind of their sighs— (1.44–1.45ab)

Those whose faces, turning dark, bear the semblance of smoke, are worthy of homage. Whom do the forest-like faces of the great-souled ones— not casting off their heart-delighting shade even when surrounded by fire— not relieve of the burden of their distress?
There were certain fortunate ones who, having made this earth fulfilled, departed for the third heaven;

I know that they left behind the proclamation of their own names here only to ward off the misfortunes of people. Whence comes this practice of the great, that even without speaking, they bring about benefit?
"Indeed, they have observed the production of fruit by trees even without flowers.
Examine this for a long time: those born of noble lineage never deviate from their own nature.
Even when shaken here and there, a fan manifests coolness upon one's limbs."
That a virtuous man shows indifference toward a wicked man who reviles him—I understood the reason for that:
because he possesses but one tongue, he cannot overcome this double-tongued man by means of stratagems.
(1.50) For those whose minds and actions are untouched by the weight of pride, forgiveness [prevails]. (1.51ab)

Why do the wicked desire to provoke quarrels with those of noble birth who possess that same single essence? Are they incapable? Alas, the number of the unrighteous has increased, while the virtuous on this earth are but two or three.
Or rather, there are serpents at every step; yet, in some places, there are life-restoring medicines.
Oh, how inconceivable is the audacity of this wicked man, possessed of such great delusion! For, though he is solely skilled in the art of slander, he considers himself to be omniscient.
Indeed, neither a base person nor a sword abandons its inherent nature, even when cherished by being placed within a sheath.
For one who is excessively defiled in nature, passion arises precisely while causing another to be split asunder in two.
Both the wicked and the crows, by their very nature, find pleasure in the sport of crushing what has been torn apart by others;
they both discharge reproachful speech and excrement alike, whether upon a worthy recipient or an unworthy one.
What is the use of these various pictures of the world’s misdeeds painted here upon my mind?

(1.56ab) For those who are adept at observing the faults of others, their own tongues are already a manifest canvas for all events. (1.56cd) Better is a wretched man who commits an open injury; one who acts with hidden malice is truly beyond remedy. (1.57ab)
People cast away a blazing fire from afar, yet they realize it has burned their feet only when it is concealed.

(1.57cd) Though capable of speaking like a rogue, a man of noble birth certainly does not manifest slander against others. (1.58ab) Though its beak is sharper than a crow’s, the parrot does not gnaw upon bones. (1.58cd)
The tongue of the wicked, though reddened by betel as a mark of royal favor, does not inspire fear in anyone;
rather, it is like a butcher’s knife, crimson with the blood dripping from the wounds of countless living beings.
Even one whose nature is pure inevitably becomes otherwise through association with unrighteous people. (1.59–1.60ab)
For even a life-sustaining medicine, when accompanied by poison, rises up to take away life.

(1.60cd) He who always provides a covering for the vital points in an assembly, though he destroys the people—he is to be praised, whether his inner disposition is wicked or not, and whether he is of noble birth or not. (1.61)
Generally, we are so preoccupied with the investigation of the Vedas that we are not similarly devoted to poetry.
Nevertheless, even though this path is difficult, those who have set out upon it while stumbling should not be neglected by poets.
For who else, however highly enlightened, could compose a literary work entirely free from corrupt words?
Even that first poet, in the course of creation, met with errors through the guile of the wicked.

(1.63cd) I have undertaken this labor of poetry for the delight of those who are deeply learned, but not for those who, by their cleverness in explaining the meaning of mere aphorisms, have surpassed even the Creator himself. (1.64)

There was a king named Suratha in the lineage of Caitra, who was comparable to the friend of Caitra (the month of Caitra). Because his enemies' army could not withstand him in battle—as if out of shame at the identity of their own name—he was like the month of Caitra itself. Fortune attended upon him without distinction, as if he were the eleventh incarnation of the beloved of Śrī (Viṣṇu).
Covered with the dust arising from the battlefields and purified by the ritual ablutions of horse-sacrifices,
the sun makes the earth free from darkness at the proper time, and the rain-cloud likewise pours down;
yet the constant activity of this Giver is for the uninterrupted protection of the world.
Fear arose only from the injury of dharma; his beloved was the very staff of his bow, naturally curved.
Greed was merely the seizing of the fortune of his enemies, and for him, fame alone was that which could not be given away.
By bestowing wealth beyond their desires upon those who approached him, he—who was the sole abode of self-respect—[attained his ends].
Even though his desire for wealth had long since departed, it was cast behind him by the sounds of his own acceptance [of renunciation].

(1.69cd) That very task which the tortoise, the serpent, the lord of the fish, the wish-fulfilling tree, the thought-gem, and the cow of plenty perform together, he alone performed—He who is the Indra of the circle of the earth. (1.70ab–1.70cd)
He, who was preeminent in noble deeds, bestowed upon the twice-born a gift of elephants and horses that was neither meager nor hollow;
by the pretext of smearing his forehead with sandalwood paste, he erased the inscription of poverty. Having rendered the virtuous penniless, the Creator became truly filled with remorse.

Therefore, as if to uproot this tree that was like a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpadruma*), he [the king] fashioned this [sword]. "Are these subjects dull-witted? Or is it some unique power of this lord, since they praise his fame for being white through its attachment to virtues, yet his two arms for being dark? (1.72cd–1.73)
From this ocean of milk, which abounds in living beings, there has arisen a certain moon of glory.
At its rising, the fame of his adversaries—fickle and moving at will—is cast aside.
The mass of their glory here does not even now decay, despite being consumed by the elixirs of praise.
Among that assembly of the best of kings, he was the one for whom the wise calculated [the limit];
by him, having conquered his enemies, that fame was acquired which follows the daughter of Urvaśī as she departs,
until the Milky Ocean, as if having reached its boundary, rolls back with its waves.

"O Goddess Vāṇī, you alone are the knower of tastes for me; therefore, praise his hand—this hand which, though possessing only five branches, surpassed the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) with its thousand branches through the glory of its generosity. Though seated upon a bull and having destroyed his enemies and desires, he is another supreme lord on earth. (1.77–78ab)

His pair of feet was worshipped by the king of mountains, and his supreme passion for the city shone forth. Having traversed the entire circle of the earth, he somehow attained such sovereignty that even these lords of the quarters remained stationed within their respective boundaries as if by his command alone.

The splendor of his enemies, who lay in the forest, burned his heart when remembered; and the spreading breath from the sighs of his beloveds, sleeping on a bed of creepers by his side, scorched his back— since the host of adversaries was fleeing from him as he glared with brows knitted in wrath upon his forehead.
Having cast aside his own lawful royal status, he instead embraced the fallen state of his distressed beloved.
Then, with the roar of his army’s elephants—
a sound that increased the thundering of the world-elephants and proclaimed the identity of heaven and earth through its resonance— he set out to conquer his enemies.

The dust raised by his advancing horses, which possessed the luster of female elephants in rut, assumed the appearance of smoke from the fire of his majesty as it scorched his enemies. Then, once the news of his arrival had been communicated to the kings by messengers, [the kings]... (1.84ab)

O King, as he advanced upon the kings who were swollen with pride— like serpents— he brought their heads, adorned with jewels, to submission by the staff of his sword; for those heads, the sandalwood paste on their foreheads had been washed away by the sweat born of terror.
Having plunged into the enemy kings' armies— which were like lakes possessing shimmering waters— he,
that preeminent king, seized their white lotuses (or royal umbrellas), like an elephant inflamed with rut;
his pale fame was illuminated by the defeat of the rival kings whose bodies were once radiant with the flow of ichor (or the splendor of their gifts).
Placing the sword-blade before him as his standard, Kṛṣṇa became victorious in battle through the power of his arms.
(1.87cd) The arrows drawn from his quiver followed the bow and then reached the chests of his enemies;
they fell upon the earth, for where indeed can there be a lasting standing for those who are devoid of merit? (1.88)

By his sword-blade, which was like the sun—rising and displaying its lotus-like hilt—the army of his enemies, along with the spreading radiance of the king’s majesty, was brought to destruction, just as the night is ended by the sun.
For who is able to restrain the intended action of one whose nature is fierce? Such indeed was that sword.

Even though he possessed elephants, he did not desist from the assembly out of avarice for his treasury; nor did he refrain from giving, even when his warders were present. (1.90cd) Some kings, casting aside their swords before him who is well-disposed toward those who bow, prostrated themselves.
(1.91ab) For those who are powerless, this alone is the remedy against death, even when [the enemy] has displayed his fury. (1.91cd)
Some kings destroyed his martial play with gifts of horses and elephants;
others, having cut off even a finger-joint, made it a protection for their remaining limbs.
There, enemies mounted upon elephants to fight turned their backs from the burden of battle.
Abandoning the conduct of a warrior, they took to the life of farmers in the forest to survive.
This man, however, being accomplished, struck down kings at the head of battle, thinking it his royal duty;

yet he was not enslaved by prosperity, which, though enjoyed many times, fails to subjugate one who has already mastered himself—just as a courtesan cannot captivate a man who is already self-controlled.
Worthy of praise is the certain cleverness of this king, since by means of his very two arms he performed that which Hari indeed accomplished with four;
for even more so than that, when he was prepared for battle, these wise men performed a difficult feat of self-preservation even at the cost of their all, using blades of grass held in their mouths.
Some were bound, some were made to bow, some were enslaved, some were cast down, some were pacified, and some were elevated.

By him, whose touch reached the furthest limits of the undertaking of universal conquest, even the kings—though their two arms were ill-behaved in their zeal for the art of caressing the sword—[were subdued].
Thus ends the first canto, titled "The Description of Suratha," in the great poem named *Surathotsava*, composed by Śrī Someśvaradeva, the priest of the illustrious Gurjareśvara.
His army, exhausted by the toil of countless marches, though restrained by those skilled in policy,
nevertheless set forth, impelled by fate, with the intent to destroy the enemies who had destroyed Kolā.
Though they were difficult to capture even for that powerful king, they were seized as they stood upon the mountain peaks.
For what can even a furious lion do against men mounted upon elephants?
Then, certain ministers of low birth, desiring to enjoy his royal fortune, instigated his enemies by means of secret incitement;
and those foes, together with him, unleashed an unrighteous assault during the night.
In that great battle, while the great warriors were being struck down by treacherous stratagems,
those informants of your lord quickly withdrew, leading back the remainder of their own army.
That hero did not indeed disregard even his enemy forces, for he was not one who lacked soldiers when an opportunity was seized by his foes.

For can even a spark of fire be touched with the tip of a finger by the one whose source is the sacrificial fire-pit? (2.5cd) Before his arm, though accompanied by his hand, could even descend toward the earth as if it were a vow he had undertaken, (2.6ab) then the tutelary deity of his own lineage, like a mother, appeared to him in a dream and spoke thus: (2.6cd)
"O great hero, withdraw alone; do not fulfill the desires of your enemies.
When fate strikes with merciless wrath, who can rise up to strike back?
Therefore, for the sake of our purpose, remain unobserved and dispel these gloomy days."
"By some time or other, you shall become powerful again," she said, and then vanished.
The king also, not being very cheerful, yet considering it at dawn to be the command of his family deity,
with great difficulty gave orders for the women of the inner apartments to go to their respective mothers' houses.
Then, having further distressed his own wealth there for the sake of awakening himself,
and having forbidden the rest under some pretext, he set out alone for the forest, unobserved by the world.
Then, even though she had been abandoned in the palace by Fortune, she followed him under the guise of his own radiance.
Having deposited his own virtues within the hearts of the virtuous, the performer of a thousand sacrifices departed for the sacrificial session.
Having seized the royal fortune through treachery toward their master, those ministers became celebrants of their own festival;
they did not foresee the destruction of their own lineage, for the sight of such men does not perceive what is so [coming].
While the vine-women began their dance and the *kīcaka* reeds resounded with the wind,
as the king entered that forest, it appeared as if a musical performance had commenced.
Alas, where is such a sovereign empire, and where is such a dwelling in the wilderness?
Whatever is difficult to accomplish even in a dream, that Fate ordains without any effort.

(2.14cd) In the forest interiors where peacocks are intoxicated with joy, and on the sandy banks where swans sport gracefully—nowhere does he find any diversion for his mind, like an elephant separated from its herd. (2.15)
Beholding at evening the edge of the forest thick with darkness, his throat choked with tears and his palace filled with longing,
he held those birds in high esteem who had made their nests there.
His bed was a bower, his garment the bark of trees, the herd of deer his friends, and fruits and roots his food.
In the forest, that lord of the earth, being without sensual objects, was like the lord of sages (the Buddha).
Entering the interior of the forests, which were dense with continuous rows of trees,
he shone like the moon emerging from a mass of clouds into circles of thick clouds that resemble crushed collyrium.
Then that lord of the earth, with a weary mind, beheld the hermitage— made precious by sages whose sins were destroyed,
and sanctified by the smoke of sacrificial fires rising from wings that served as moons for those who longed to see;
it was filled with herds of cows ever-present and with pure, radiant brahmins.
There, the leaf-huts of the lotus-seated Brahmā attained a likeness to his own lotus-face;
having performed their fire-rites with faith and reaching perfection through the application of the *niṣṭhā* suffix,
the sages who rose from there were like grammarians intent upon the *parasmaipada*.

In that place, the daughters of the great sages bore joy through the gift of wild rice to the young deer, by the act of watering the young forest trees, and by the marriage of the *mādhavī* creepers; there,
he whose slender body was graced with the beauty of gold had his feet washed by the waters of the best of rivers.
There, the dark-hued foliage of the trees assumed the seal of Upendra.
There, parrots, constantly uttering the words heard from the Vedas,
wandered about eating fruits at the foot of Viṣṇu’s tree, as if receiving instruction from the lords of ascetics.

The source of the Vedas, the enemy of the senses, the abundance of purity, and the abode of compassion—for those dwelling in the desert of saṃsāra, he was indeed a lake; in him there once lived the sage Sumedhas.
Once, that sage of sharp intellect went into that penance grove for the sake of sacrificial wood and *kuśa* grass.

He gazed upon that lord of elephants, who was being watched by deer with tearful eyes and who bore a state of distress. He whom he had previously seen, lovely to behold and possessing a beauty as enchanting as a herd of elephants,
now stood there with his heart agitated upon seeing him wandering alone in the forest.
Seeing the Lord of Ascetics thus situated, his form exalted by a special radiance,

the king, impelled by his own inner heart, bowed down while offering his own name. Having prostrated before that sage who had raised his hand in blessing, the moon among kings, with a joyful soul, paid him homage.

He considered his own prosperity as already attained, for the company of the virtuous is a guarantor of future abundance. Then that sage of noble intellect, having brought the moon of the earth to his hermitage where even the wild beasts were watchful, offered him hospitable honors; for the great, though they have fallen from worldly wealth, remain worthy of honor.

Having honored him with water for his feet and the offering of *arghya*—having offered the foot-water with water for the feet and the *arghya* with the *arghya*—the great-souled sage, sharing in a similar sorrow, questioned the king whose lotus-face was lusterless. (2.31) He questioned those two who had attained a reddish hue from the splendors of the crest-jewels of the rows of bowing kings. (2.32)

Alas, why do these feet of yours bear the wounds inflicted by the tips of darbha grass? Why was your face so clouded with dust that mingled with the sweat of your brow— dust which, though more painful than even for kings, was not seen by the monarchs who were turned away at the gate as they approached to pay their respects?
Is that shoulder of yours, renowned for granting rest to the Lord of Serpents who was bent under the burden of the earth,
marked by the tips of thorns which resemble the nail-scratches inflicted by the bride of calamity?
Upon it fell a rain of flowers released joyfully by the gods in battle.

Why is this crest of yours, worthy of a crown, piled with blades of grass clinging to the surface of the earth? That cluster of calluses from the bowstring upon your golden arm—which rivals the luster of a sapphire—is seen upon limbs that share the common nature of time; why is it not regarded as distinct [from the rest]?
Thus questioned by the Lord of Sages with charming speech,
the king— whose long arms were like the poles of a chariot and whose throat was choked with shame— related his sorrow experienced in the past.
Having heard the cause of the monarch’s misfortunes and desiring to restore for him the festival of sovereignty once more, [the Sage spoke].
For the virtuous are singularly devoted to the task of relieving the suffering of the world; thus he made his resolve.
Only that daughter of the Mountain King is capable of restoring his sovereignty to him.
Realizing this through his wisdom, that treasury of knowledge then began to speak to him.
Indeed, one should not be distressed by separation from what is good, for alas, the great endure everything;
who indeed has not fallen into this snare of fate, even while seeking the path of the virtuous? For the course of destiny is beyond the reach of both the good and the wicked.
With the splendor of gold, he freely places upon his head either a crown or a turban.
(2.41cd) Neither valor, nor noble birth, nor learning, nor charm, nor youth, nor conduct—this adverse fate, once it has begun its course, does not require any of these for the ruin of men. (2.42)
A wise man does not create openings through which others may enter;
yet, Yama, the Ender, moves about by means of whatever opening he finds, for he alone knows it.
When that Creator obstructs men, he then afflicts them in whatever way possible.

In that regard, alas! those who desire to seize by means of evil that fortune which is obtainable only through virtue— that fortune which consists in the laying down of the weapon of mere benevolence toward one who seeks to kill—
are like those who strive to trace the path through the forest, visible in the daylight, by means of darkness.

Granted that wealth may sometimes be acquired by men through unwholesome actions, yet if it is opened up by base means within its own source, it will not be auspicious in the end, like honey [placed] in a jar. Even if one is liberated from even a slight fault, provided it is solely through greedlessness...
I suspect that Fortune, filled with longing as if born of remorse, will seek his lap once again.
Generally, even when the Creator displays his wrath toward those of noble conduct, it is imbued with gentleness—
just as the summer heat, though fierce as the sun of Bhīṣma, is tempered by the trees on the path providing thick shade.
O Lord of the Earth, without delay, worship the Mother of the Three Worlds, the consort of the Lord of Beings;
for she, who is compassionate toward her devotees, will swiftly bestow auspiciousness upon you.
She who is the single seed of the worlds, and who has been placed in the hearts of yogis by those whose actions are directed toward no other end.
Hear now of the power of this consort of Śarva, who is the deity even of the gods.

"May there be no blow upon the heads of those who dwell above the world by this rod of punishment!
Surely, fearing [this] in their minds, the kings wait upon you with great reverence as they bow down.
O Danuja, your affection for your subjects exceeds even that of Daśānana, who had conquered Duścyavana."
Since you are known for the severing of your own head rather than the severing of the heads of others,
when your name is proclaimed by others through poetic compositions,
the two hands of the lords of the directions— dropping their weapons as their heads bow down— fall away from their grasp. (8.16cd–8.17)
Furthermore, while they are unable to challenge you out of regard for your sovereignty over the world,
the lords of the quarters consider that entering into your service is the only effective means for their own welfare.
Desiring to cast [the garland] upon the head of you, the victor in the arenas of battle, they seek your favor.
"Even upon the celestial tree, there is a thinness of flowers that are gathered by the immortals at every moment.
Moreover, O Lord, listen with undivided attention to another marvel perceived by me;
for when a man is intent on listening, the growth of the speaker's thought gains further excellence."
Urged with curiosity by that Lord, whose two ears were intent on hearing,
the messenger delivered words that were like poison— painful in their ultimate consequence yet pleasing at first.
"There stands a mountain renowned throughout the three worlds as Himavat, as white as the loud laughter of Giriśa."
Like Śeṣa, who—having placed the earth upon the lord of tortoises—seems to desire to support the heavens from his uplifted hood;

on the peak of that lord of mountains, there is a certain woman with the luster of gold, bestowing upon the God of the Uneven Arrows the consecration for the conquest of the three worlds with drops of the nectar of her laughter. (8.22cd–8.23)
Her charming face, with its radiant halo of light from her jeweled earrings shimmering all around, practices the beauty of the moon encircled by a lunar halo. She,
whose lovely eyes are like blooming lotuses, shines with a fresh necklace of pearls upon her neck.
As if a stream of nectar were falling from within the orb of her moon-like face, cool to the touch,

delightful with swans in the form of sweet voices, and filled with *khañjarīṭa* birds in the form of many side-glances— she shines forth exceedingly, like the very embodiment of autumn, as the cause for awakening the God of Love.

The steadiness of her speech, the mobility of her eyes, the fullness of her breasts, and the downward curve of her shoulders; (8.27ab) the slender waist of her belly and the abundance of her hips—nowhere else is such a thing to be found. (8.27cd) Fortunate is that father and blessed is that mother, for whom this daughter is the fruit of their womb, a vessel of auspiciousness. (8.28ab)
I consider that man alone to be one who has crushed the pride of the god of love, since she rests upon his lap.
Was her body, with its luster capable of being held in a cupped palm, poured out from the orb of the moon?
Or was it fashioned by the Creator in his mind, so that that glory might not be defiled by the touch of a hand?
If you desire that youth be fruitful, and if you wish for this great sovereignty and life itself to be meaningful,
O Lord, then take without delay into your hand that lotus-born one from the lake of beauty—
she who is lovely with eyes like restless black antelopes, adorned with ears like the tips of grass-blades, and graced by rows of teeth like a flight of birds.
"Let that body of yours become an ascetic hermitage for the God of Love, for the sake of your own liberation.

(8.31cd) Thus, with his heart lusted by the power of those words, he—who was the cause of distress to the world—was at last reached by both Madana and Destiny as the opportunity to strike him arose. (8.32ab-8.32cd)
Urged by the haste instilled by Love, that enemy of the gods, his mind still attached to the woman,
was commanded once more by his friend to win over the daughter of the mountain king— a task that befriended him in his unrighteousness.
Sent there for that purpose by his master, the servant of the Flower-Armed God, he was to accomplish a deed achievable through a friend.
With a mind intoxicated by passion, this messenger went to the snowy mountain abode.
Having performed a prostration with his head before the wife of the City-Crusher,
he— acting as a messenger— manifested the power of his own lord’s arm, which was the seed of abundant affection.

"O Goddess, listen to what Śumbha has said through my mouth, and having reflected upon it, follow his word—he who, surpassing the lords of the worlds, is worshipped by Lakṣmī for his beautiful form and virtues.
(8.36) The kings, possessing hearts that have captivated the God of Love, bear a withered splendor upon their faces. (8.37)

Like those afflicted by fever, they find no comfort anywhere... [it] cuts me like the heat of my own majesty. (8.37cd) Having first considered that wretched succession of enemy kings who are devoid of compassion, though I am addicted to the slaughter of enemies, I do not cast aside my group of merciless arrows in battle. (8.38ab–cd)

During my world-conquest, the sky—darkened by the masses of dust raised by the surging flood of my advancing army—was perceived as night; meanwhile, the austerities performed by rival kings were rendered fruitless because they lacked the heat [of sovereignty]. But for those arrogant monarchs who were utterly destroyed by the dense volleys of my falling arrows...
Upon the crest of battle, I shall adorn this earth with shaven heads, [the forms] of those whose crowns are the moon.
(8.40cd) Daily bearing hearts sluggish in pride, envy, and passion, like those of yogis, these Maruts, having been devoured by men, now swiftly desire release from their bonds. (8.41ab–cd)

Having heard my lion’s roar, raised high in battle—which causes the herds of elephants that are my enemies to tremble—the deer, out of fear, have become like mere deer as they wander within the depths of mountain caves. I do not slay Yama, who holds his staff; nor do I have any concern for the King of the Kinnaras, the messenger of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
Varuṇa, having brought his own vessel near, obstructed my firm resolve in battle.
(8.43cd) Those whose minds are intent on slaying their enemies pay homage to me, whose splendor has disregarded all insults.
(8.44ab) The Vasus honor me with the fruits produced by the celestial trees; for the service of a husband is indeed appropriate for women. (8.44cd)

That chest of mine, which no multitude of weapons—beginning with the thunderbolt hurled by the gods—could ever touch, now these arrows of Smara torment, O slender-limbed one, as you are full of passion for me. While I remain here... [O lady] with lips like coral, [I possess] the jewel of trees, the jewel of elephants, and the jewel of horses.
"Moreover, among women, I long to take as my wife one who is like a jewel.
(8.46cd) While I, the best of heroes, am here, you ought not, O lady with hair like peacock feathers, to go to another man.
(8.47ab) Would a fine gem, having cast aside gold, ever place its affection upon tin? (8.47cd)
Having made both the fish-bannered god of love and myself identical in form with his own heart through prostration, the Creator then churned us two like the god of love and left only one remaining;
this was certain. [And so it was] for the goddesses whose transgressions are restrained by men, and for the moon-faced women among the gods who have Agni as their mouth.
Your pleasure, O noble lady, is not suited to those joined with serpents who are devoid of sacred learning, like [the pleasure] of Śūdras.
Roaming with a husband of unbearable prowess, like the goddess dwelling in the lotus with Hari,
enjoy this abundance of the forest, O slender one, in these Vindhya woods that are the kinsmen of Madhu.

"Swiftly I have conquered this manly power, while you, by your loveliness, have subdued feminine beauty. Let these two of ours, joined together, be invincible even to the world, for we are equal in our respective powers.
[Let them be the prize] of the beauties of gods among men and gods among serpents, whose husbands are terrified by my prowess."
"O blessed lady, become one whose lotus-feet are to be venerated by those who desire the alms of their husband's life.
If you have no affection for me, who am fierce in my prowess, then resort to my younger brother, the auspicious Niśumbha— you,
a young woman with passion restrained, like a night-lily seeking the moon, which is easy to enjoy."
Having heard those words, the Goddess, harboring anger within her heart yet displaying outward composure,
shone all the more— like a *śamī* tree containing fire within it and putting forth new sprouts.
Then, with a voice that shared the beauty of the resonance of the lute of the Goddess of Speech, [she spoke].
The young woman spoke with respect to him, whose ornament was a fragment of the moon:
"O dear one, that which you have spoken is indeed consistent with the prowess of your own lord;
for the lord of Indra’s elephant himself, when stripped of his rut, is the witness to the arrogance of Śumbha."
By me, through supreme wisdom, a great vow was already established long ago.
Listen to that as well—it is in every way not to be abandoned, like the battlefield of great warriors.
Even if he is devoid of virtues, even if he carries a skull-bowl, even if he belongs to a lineage ignorant of the truth, and even if he is without support—
"He is my husband, who was chosen by me as I stepped forward together with the lioness;
how then can this vow, once made with a resolute mind, be rendered false?
For this indeed is the mark of the great-souled: that their words never deviate."

"Let that lord of the Dānavas, or the younger brother of that foremost of Danujas, come here; or let him, devoted to equal combat, go quickly to the abode of Yama with his body adorned for battle. Having received these words, so unbecoming of a woman, with his ears, the Daitya-possessed one [listened].
He spoke again with a jest to her whose long eyes were like the petals of a blooming blue lotus:

"Even if there were a tongue in your mouth and it were under your control, and if you did not speak excessively when censured, nevertheless, O wise one, you should speak in accordance with what is well-composed; for the learned place their trust in speech that is logical. (8.61cd–8.62)
O charming one, you are made an object of pity by this circle of friends who are intent on showing you affection—
those who do not restrain you, even by force, as you thus prattle on so devoid of reason.
O lady with limbs as tender as a plantain leaf, [you are being restrained] by him who is as hard as the strike of a proud enemy’s elephant-tusk.
I am amazed that you, O timid woman, desire a battle with that powerful warrior;
for the gods do not venture into combat against him whose arms are as fierce as the thunderbolt.
That even a helpless woman wishes to oppose him—to you, O Delusion, be homage!
"O girl, abandon this arrogance; let your eye, which is full of passion for me, be forcibly drawn here.
Let my request bear fruit, and let even the god [Śiva] bring about your destruction rather than out of disrespect.
Furthermore, I consider this to be a cause for the humiliation of my husband, even though he is powerful."
"Having contemplated you, who are worthy of honor, he will certainly become one who is no longer even master of himself.
Having correctly understood that her resolve could not be turned back by words, the follower of the lord of the Daityas reached Mount Revā,
where the collection of rocks is purified by the river, in less time than the blink of an eye.

He related in brief to her husband— who was eager to approach that woman whose eyes possessed lashes like those of a doe with fierce glances— the haughtiness of the group of women, which was contrary to their nature. At the conclusion of the spy’s report, that wanderer, desiring to see the son of Diti who was capable of victory over him, [departed].
With his soul surrendered to passion and envy, he cast his gaze, uplifted, upon the assembly.
Was the Asura deluded by prosperity as if it were wine, or by sense-objects that resemble poison, that he did not perceive Death standing right before him in the guise of a woman? (8.70cd–8.71)

Fickle by nature and full of passion, her brow was curved like a garland; his gaze fell upon that daughter of the Daityas—named Dhūmralocanā—just as a woman of loose conduct fixes her eyes upon a paramour who is not even present. Then, [he beheld her] who had swallowed the weight of the waters of the ocean being churned by Mount Mandara.
He, whose mountain was made to resound by that sound, spoke these words requested with humility:
"O hero, you alone possess the power of arms that is the sole support for my body;
therefore, bring this beloved one from the lord of mountains as a medicine to cure my fever of love."

If you do not first consider the means, even though you are full of pride, you will resort to the fourth [alternative]. (8.75ab) If anyone shows partiality toward you who are desirous of battle, that is pleasing to one born for war.
(8.75cd) Thereafter, being prepared even at the cost of your own life through the conduct of a hero honored by your lord— (8.76ab)
He rose up with elegance, intent on quickly bringing that wife of the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Veiling the mass of the sun’s rays and muddying even the waters of the oceans with the spreading dust raised by his horses,
that Daitya reached the king of mountains with speed.
Like a moth flying into a flame, the Asura pounced upon that beloved of the enemy of the cities (Śiva), who was illuminating everything around her with her own golden web of rays.
And he said this: "O fair-eyed one, you have the choice between two things to be done here according to your will."
"Obtain existence from the one preceded by 'dvi' (two) when he is pleased, or from the one preceded by 'pari' (around) when the son of Diti is not pleased. Then,
while Kaca, his words rendered fruitless, was enraged and sought to pull her hair, she,
uttering a roar of defiance (*huṃkāra*), reduced him to ashes— his death having been brought about by his own karma.

When that army had been reduced to ashes by Bhavānī and the followers of the bridegroom were swiftly destroyed, she alone became the protection for the Ādityas, who were distressed by fear of the Daityas; she herself became their safeguard. Thus ends the eighth canto, titled "The Slaying of Dhūmralocana," in the great poem named *Surathotsava*, composed by Śrī Someśvaradeva, the priest of the Lord of Gurjara.
Ninth Canto: By that report concerning the Daitya, this leader of the enemies of the gods,
pained and enraged, then began to strike with his staff like a serpent with its coils.
His high braid of hair shone like a ripe stalk of grain,
appearing as if it had risen up, piercing through his head like a flame from the fire of his wrath.
His limbs, with beads of sweat breaking forth, gleamed brilliantly.
As if they had accepted water out of fear of being scorched by the fire of his wrath,
and thinking with trepidation, "He will soon bite me with his teeth," I believe the lip of that enraged man was quivering.
On the forehead of the fierce lord of the Daityas, named Aruṇa,
which was naturally terrifying with its frown, his anger was clearly visible.
Śumbha [addressed] those seated in the assembly, whose pride was undiminished and whose heat of passion had not yet subsided.

Enraged, he assigned them their respective portions as if they were his own splendors. Beholding the eldest of them blazing with his own brilliance like the month of Āṣāḍha, Niśumbha, out of wrath, endeavored to bear that heat.
He was exceedingly terrifying due to a contraction of his eyebrows, raised in a surge of anger that resembled the curved horns of a black antelope;
he bore a bristling of the hair produced by his engagement in battle.
Like one cat provoked by another cat, the demon Cāmara was incensed by Vṛṣādviṣa.
In his rage, he shook his tail;
from that first movement, the three worlds trembled with fear.
Enraged, the courier likewise struck his own shank with his hand,
so that it became even redder than blood from sheer fury.
Raktabīja, already red as the seeds of a ripe guñjā berry, became even more so out of rage.
Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa became [respectively] Muṇḍa and Caṇḍa with a sense of urgency;
though they had not even taken up their armor, they were rendered armored by their fury.
Pīṭhaka, rising from his seat, was held up with great difficulty by others.
Brandishing in his hand a sword that had never before rescued an enemy,
he— though usually mute— through rage made himself known as one who longs for battle.
Then, out of indignation toward the others who were delaying their departure...
With his sharp-edged tongue, he uttered a stinging taunt;
and at the onset of the battle's commencement,
the face of the wrathful Durmukha, bearing a look of defiance, turned toward him.
Dhenuka, armed with his sword and cow-tail whip,
repeatedly gazed with eyes like sparks of fire upon the quarter of the world sealed by the Himalayas.
Bāṣkala, though intoxicated with pride, maintained a longing for battle.
His mind was slightly troubled by doubt, thinking, "Is this not Arāti?
The assembly of the lord of the Daityas became crimson with the wrath of the Daityas,
like the earth streaked with red chalk by the elephants of Mount Vindhya.
Then Śumbha, resembling a fresh cloud,
rose from his lion-throne adorned with gold, like smoke from a fire.
As he was rising from the seat, his foot stumbled.
"Rushing toward what was not its task, my mind has first stumbled"—
having perceived this as a great ill omen for the Lord, the minister Maya, who knew the signs, then spoke these words appropriate to the occasion.
"O Lord of Heroes, take up the auspicious seat once again;
for honored omens honor those very things as well.
[9.23] [He saw him] seated again upon that golden throne, once more on the verge of calamity. [9.24ab]
Though filled with apprehension, the best of ministers spoke without hesitation:
"O Lord, we who know all branches of learning—what are we in your presence?
Nevertheless, this devotion toward you impels me to speak."

It is a marvel that those who tame kings—who, like elephants, have gone astray through excessive pride—should live for so long. O King, you must forgive what I am about to say, for these words are spoken by one who is trustworthy. (9.26–9.27ab)
In the beginning it is as painful as austerity, yet at the end it becomes desirable.
A minister appointed to his post attains renown through speech that is either bitter or sweet, just as a physician of Āyurveda gains fame through the application of emetics or tonics.
The speech of ministers is like the mango fruit:
it possesses sweetness at first, yet is accompanied by a certain pungency at the end. People who speak only pleasant words at first cause torment in the end. (9.29–9.30ab)
One must fear even water as it flows, like a variegated rain-cloud.
O King, you alone are expert in the scriptures and in weapons;
why then do you so hastily proceed toward a matter whose true nature is unknown?
He alone deceives Fortune, who is as fickle as the waves of the ocean—(9.32ab)—he who, though himself clever, remains standing after having intended to act among the wise.
(9.32cd) "Who is she? To whom does she belong? Or why does she stand here all alone?"—thus [he asks] with his voice. (9.33ab)

Having thus determined, he should proceed to undertake the task with diligence. Like a king who is a patron of sacrifice, he clearly enjoys the desired fruit through divine rites performed according to rule and preceded by mantras.
"This woman's attire is unwholesome for us; surely this has arisen [as a portent].
Thus does my mind, overcome by agitation, speak as it were.
Even women tremble at battle more than at a figure depicted in a painting.
That she desires to fight even with you—this is indeed a marvel!
O Lord, casting aside your agitation, consider this as well:
for is a cowherd not praised, O King, by one who lacks discernment? (9.36cd–9.37)
Moreover, O Hero,
even Brahmā, at the moment of bestowing his boons, granted you victory in battle— save for your bride.
O Lord, I see her here, possessed of boundless valor, as if she were that very goddess herself.
"Women pierce the heart with their gestures, not indeed with weapons.
(9.39cd) This [criticism] is not appropriate for you, who follow the path of the poets.
O Lord, in poetry alone does such behavior toward women exist, like the use of grass [as a mere pretext]. (9.40ab–9.40cd)
Why indeed were you not defeated in battle by that [arrow],
since you were pierced even by the flower-arrows of Kandarpa, which are as firm as a thunderbolt?
Today, let the arrogant Kandarpa revel with pride before the dwellers of heaven.
By this [power], even you, though previously unsubmissive, have been brought by force into a state of obedience.
(9.42cd) For men abiding in sovereign power or performing supreme austerity, the restraint of the collection of the senses is the cause of success. (9.43ab–9.43cd)

Granted, she too was conquered by you; yet what fame is there for you in the conquest of a woman? (9.44ab) Furthermore, what distinction is there in one who, considering it death, challenges it himself? (9.44cd) One who is superior cannot be conquered, nor is there fame in conquering the lowly. (9.45ab)
In battle with an equal, there is doubt; therefore, for men, forbearance is the highest forbearance. (9.45cd) Let this [forbearance] be resorted to, and let the mind be drawn away from hatred.
For this is indeed seen to be the fruit of the vision of the scriptures: the path of what ought to be done. (9.46ab–9.46cd)
"Turn back from this undertaking of impurity; be gracious to me.
O Lord, do not show me the door of Fate, who watches for a vulnerability.
He who, out of pride, behaves wickedly while his kinsmen are groaning [in distress]..."

By means of cruel punishment inflicted by fate, he is brought to his senses through force. Though awakened by that [punishment], he did not perceive for himself what was beneficial; for discernment does not set foot upon a fool, just as one afraid of the mud does not place a foot in it.
Wasting his words like one about to die who refuses medicine,
he of the terrifying form, the king of those hostile to the consumer of nectar (the moon),
spoke that which was worthy of the conduct of a friend and appropriate for one of great learning.
And that speech which you uttered was appropriate for a counselor;
for he who is eloquent reveals the underlying meaning as if displaying it before one's eyes.
He is a true friend who personally receives the calamity falling upon his companion.
The intellect is refined by the scriptures and is well-instructed by the elders;
yet there is another kind of good fortune entirely, by which the glory of victory is enjoyed.
Know that there are four branches of knowledge as well as their corresponding means.

Without singular valor, the mind does not advance toward the enemy. (9.54cd) If even one who knows no truth can shake the heads of his foes, tell me, by whom was wisdom bestowed upon the lion in battle? (9.55ab–cd)
For those arrogant in their excellence of manhood, the restraint of the scriptures is useless;
for what restriction can there be on food for those whose digestive fires are unassailable?
It is no fault that I was conquered by that woman, even though I am a man. (9.56–9.57ab)
In this matter, the failing intellect of one such as you is at fault for your old age.
(9.57cd) Since I have split even the pair of frontal globes of Śakra’s elephant, that very same I shall surely be terrified by the pair of a woman’s breasts! (9.58ab–9.58cd)
If this [conduct] is to be suspected by us, then it should be practiced all the more;
for that wise man who remains fearless toward others even when there is a cause for fear, [he is truly steadfast].
That which is sung as *sāman* by the brahmins, and that which is called *dāna*, arises from grace.
"I know how to break the chest of a thief or an enemy; I am skilled in punishment. Yet, though afflicted by desire, I do not wish to seize this woman.
For the lord of the earth is entitled to take everything that belongs to no one."
A proud man does not bend his upraised head before an enemy; he would rather have it severed while walking upon the earth. What is the use of that life obtained by bowing down to an enemy?
Even death is encountered by him who approaches while cutting down his enemies.
You remain unhurt by one whose very nature is to wound; this is security for those such as you.
For heroes, even their speech is like the fire of valor and difficult to endure, how much more so their actual action?
It is the consensus of those who compose sūtras when refuting the doctrines of others:
"Is there not even a slight degree of lightness for those whose very life is their pride?
Therefore, I shall surely destroy that [pride], or let it destroy me in this assembly.

For among heroes, the cutting off of the nose is more unbearable than the cutting off of the head. What has not been achieved by that hero who, having sacrificed himself within the midst of battle, caused even his enemies—such as Durmukha—to sing his own praises? (9.66cd–9.67)

Having uttered these words, like an elephant in rut casting off its garland, he rose from his throne, having commenced a conflict at an improper time. Then, with a voice as terrible as the roar of an aged thundercloud...
He quickly commanded the soldiers to prepare the army. At his command, the wicked ones of the gods set forth unrestrained, like the waves of the ocean driven by the winds at the end of an aeon.
"Armor! Armor! Weapon! Weapon! Chariot!
Chariot!"—thus were the shouts of the formidable, great warriors heard on all sides.
Adorned with their variegated armor, those heroes shone resplendently.
Like mountains trembling when struck by the rays of the rising sun,
[the kings] were shaken. Because he had no regard for her as a mere woman, Viśva-kaṇṭaka, urged on by others, took up his armor with limbs bristling with martial ardor.
Surrounded by the Maruts who held swords in their hands, he experienced,
as it were, while still alive, the state of dwelling in a forest of sword-leaves.
Jayanta was then hurled by the partisans of Śumbha into the ranks of the horses.
Victory will not come to the deluded, but rather to the Self;
for those elephants which were fashioned by the Daityas for battle,
they were in fact fashioned by Fate for the God of Death without any doubt.
"O Queen, do not go to that mountain," [he said] through the cries of the bees;
I believe even the elephants restrained that man intoxicated by the pride of his arms.
With the vast circle of discus-wielders as his banner... 9.78ab
And as he was about to depart for the next world,

the ground before the gate of his palace became crowded with horses equipped with armor, with chariots provided with protective fenders, and with elephants ready for action; it was as if filled with the very clouds that accompany one departing for the hereafter.

The tiger among dānavas ascended his tiger-skin-covered chariot, prepared for battle, which was equipped with weapons capable of committing hostilities against the world. It was certain that a battle would surely take place between these two, both arrogant in their prowess.
In the interval between that [sound] and the sun, a parasol was produced against the heat.
Through its immeasurable abundance, a state of nihilism was attained;
through the resonance of its soundless resonance, a state of nihilism was attained.
With the sound of kettledrums, the army set forth, pervading the quarters with its elephant corps, the earth,
and the high sky with its dust;
as Śumbha moved out, his fluttering banners appeared like a mass of disheveled hair.
He wept, as if with the sound of the marching drums of the Fortune of the Daityas.
Under the guise of the columns of dust raised by the moving and surging [army],
even the mountain, it is said, followed him in alarm.
The dust of the earth was lifted by his fierce horse-hooves as if by his austerities,
just as it had been cast down by the turbid conduct of those with elephantine rut-fluids. By him, the scorching [heat] was being released, as if by one freed from a fever of worldly existence.
The mountain shed sweat under the pretext of being sprinkled by the ichor flowing from the temples of the army’s elephants.
As the vermilion rising high from their frontal globes was fanned by the wind from their flapping ears,
it appeared as if the very quarters of the sky were on fire.
Even by the hosts of celestial beings gazing with great effort,
no end to Bala was found— neither in front, nor behind, nor on the sides.
[He was] in the great mountain caves where lions were awake, their bodies bound by the frost of the quarters.

The roar of the approaching forces of the Nivātakavacas became heavy with echoes. (9.90cd) As the army of the Daityas gradually drew near with multitudes of peacock-feather sunshades, the line of forest trees growing at the side of the lord of mountains attained great breadth. (9.91ab–91cd)

Standing upon the king of mountains, the people beheld the army— fierce with its warriors and horsemen like the powerful Indra himself— surpassing the canopy of the earth above under the guise of clouds of dust rising from the impact of the hooves of the galloping circles of horses, beyond the reach of the sun’s rays.
As the sun gazed toward the zenith of the sky, its orb was rendered pale by the mass of dust shimmering from the ground trampled by the hooves of that cavalry.

Even at midday, the host of Kinnara maidens, accompanied by the gods, descended beneath the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpadruma*) to perform auspicious rites for the Flower-Armed One (*kusumāyudha*). Thus ends the ninth canto, titled "The Departure of the Daityas," in the great poem named *Surathotsava*, composed by Śrī Someśvaradeva, the priest of the Lord of Gurjara.
The Tenth Canto.
Then, beholding that army, even the three worlds were agitated;
the Great Goddess Mahiṣī, eager for the desire to fight, became intent once more.
With her mouth wide open and her hand grasping a weapon, she stood ready.
At that festival of battle, he manifested joy and indignation;
then Pārvatī’s gaze, illuminating the quarters with its own spreading rays like a meteor, fell upon the enemy host.
The beloved of the Conqueror of Smara recalled all her own forms;
yet she remained in doubt as to whether they had come from that body or from elsewhere.
Indeed, not even one of them was able to conquer the Daityas. (10.4–10.5ab)
He desired to sever that happiness as if with all his forms.
Shining with the luster of a radiant lotus by means of the swan,
