Having cast aside her necklace, she applies sandalwood water to her chest and places a lotus leaf over it.
Even that which she has surrendered, the intoxicated woman longs to place upon the sprout of your hand.
Therefore come, O beloved, grant us our life; why is this salutation with joined palms being made?
For toward those like you, who are like the wish-fulfilling tree, the conduct of a petitioner is not in vain.
While this lord of the earth remained silent, disregarding these words of hers, she did not merely release her sighs in despair; even the fish-bannered god discharged his weapon.
When the king had rejected his companion, that illusory woman, along with the chamberlains, [departed].

She vanished, removing the despondency of those who had performed acts of devotion for the sake of attaining her beauty. (13.91cd) Then, standing in the sky, they—having cast away their flowers—boasted at the king whose chest was pierced by the arrows of the god of uneven darts, yet who possessed immense splendor: "For affection indeed increases toward one who has performed a noble deed. (13.92ab–cd)
Thus ends the thirteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Illusory Woman," in the *Kāvyaratnakaraṇḍikā* composed by the illustrious Someśvaradeva, known as the *Surathotsava*.

Then, the supreme goddess most dear to the Lord, being pleased by the king’s exceedingly great asceticism, revealed her own form which quells all suffering; for the exertion of the virtuous toward the great is never in vain. (14.1)

That which the Sage, filled with joy, had announced after long reflection with undivided mind—he, the lord of the earth, beheld that incomparable and great light shimmering before him and was struck with wonder.
"Know me, my child, to be Muditā, the sole mother of the world, because of this great vow of yours. (14.2–14.3)
"Therefore, state quickly the boon for which you have entreated me," so spoke the Mountain-Dweller (Śiva) to her.
As the daughter of the Lord of Mountains spoke thus, the dust from the toe of the Creator— who bowed with a joyful heart—
adhered to his forehead and became the royal tilaka-mark upon it.

With his head perfumed by the abundance of flowers offered by the joyful gods, and with his eyes mingled with the spray of a woman’s tears, he placed his joined palms upon it and spoke these words of joy with reverence:
“Today my birth has become auspicious; even with this body, the great fruit of ascetic practices has been swiftly realized.”
By your vision, which is itself invisible, a great fitness has been bestowed upon me.
(14.6cd) What is this that has dawned, yet the sun remains unmanifest; am I perhaps devoid of luster, or is it because of this very body?
(14.7ab) O Girijā, O Conqueror of the Enemy, I have beheld before me your lotus-feet, whose sight is never in vain. (14.7cd)

I bow to this foot of yours in the festival of battle, which, with its crimson luster as if from wrath, seized the enemy long before the strike—his foe who had already been reflected in the mirror of your nails. (14.8) There, the Discus of Hari could not advance, nor was he capable of destroying it with his thunderbolt, O Conqueror of Mountains. (14.9)

I bow to him who instantly crushed even his enemies—the one who is bowed to by the gods. Your two feet have attained a state of being worthy of prostration, eternally removing the inauspiciousness of the Maruts:
the first, which brought an end to Mahiṣa, and the other, which bound the son of Virocana for Hari.
O Goddess, even in the three worlds, this foot of yours alone is thus the granter of desired objects;
for when the Pināka-wielder, the Teacher of the World, desiring the joy of his favor, bowed down during a playful quarrel,
you bewildered him just as you did Madhu and Kaiṭabha of formidable prowess when he strode the three steps.
Even now, the Lotus-seated One sings of your glory, for the creatures dwelling within his belly [sing it].
O Daughter of the Snowy Mountain, by whom can your entire majesty be measured, with its boundless splendor?
For while some [glories] may arise from the bodies of the gods at times, you alone are the one who creates them as well.
By that radiance which had arisen, he became like the mountain Vāmana, the abode of the gods, though he was already lofty;
yet even greater than that light, your body, having destroyed the asuras, surpassed it in its vastness.
Though his weapons were claws, he remained unconquered by others who possessed sharp-edged weapons—just as the lion, despite being struck by the hooves of others, triumphs over them.

I bow to that *huṃ* uttered by you, which indeed severed Dhūmralocana in battle—that *huṃ* which, with its chowries lopped off in combat, rendered the stable sovereignty of the immortals devoid of its chowries. By you, this great sword was fashioned solely for the delight of rending enemies; though it was once effective, it has now been rendered fruitless.

Obeisance to you, who hold a tender garland of *āmalaka* fruits, O mother of Alikāyā and Mātalikā. (14.17ab) And by whom Caṇḍikā was swiftly manifested in battle at the time of the dissolution of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa.
(14.17cd) O Bhavānī, you drank the wine of blood produced from the seed of blood upon the field of battle. (14.18ab)

Then, for the nectar-eaters whose minds blossomed through the absence of sinful conduct, intoxication arose once more. When you had crushed the emperor of the Daityas, the thousand-eyed Indra— cooled by the tears from his eyes flowing with spreading joy and resembling a fountain-house— was resorted to by the Fortune of Heaven, who was tormented by him.
That state which is sought by those who fear worldly existence after long serving a man difficult to find— O gracious one,
you grant that very state even to a woman, for she is easily obtained and bows but once.
O lotus-faced one, you alone are indeed Lakṣmī, by whom, when satisfied, kingship was attained.
Even though he is a mortal, he is addressed as "God" by the throngs of his servants, and yet that title does not fail to shine upon him.
(14.21cd) O you who were born from the mouth of the elephant-faced god, those with suprasensory vision call you Sarasvatī;
for through your grace, nectar dwells within the voices of poets, while it turns into poison among the wicked. (14.22ab–14.22cd)
What could be more dear to me than this that I now request from you, whose glance is auspicious by its very nature?
Or rather, O Bhavānī, since it must inevitably be granted by you, let there simply be an abundance of devotion toward you.
(14.23) With the rays of her teeth, as beautiful as blossoming jasmine, she spreads over him a white parasol. (14.24ab)
Before the king, the beloved of the enemy of Tripura (Śiva) spoke words sweet with grace:
"O child, you of immense valor, enjoy the prosperity of your own kingdom which shall endure for a thousand years—
a kingdom that manifests for you the pain of long separation through its limbs, which remain unadorned and unembellished."
"Cast aside this rosary with this arm of yours; take up the bow for the subduing of the enemy!

Even alone, while wearing but a single bracelet of lotus fibers, you have surpassed both the lord of serpents and the wielder of the thunderbolt. Let this arm of yours, possessing unequalled power that cannot be fully realized even by the earth itself, maintain its steadfastness."
He who, fondling his formidable sword in battle, rends the hearts of his adversaries in two—
never shall there be defeat or humiliation for you on the field of combat.
Like darkness before the dawn, the circle of enemy kings will swiftly perish from your army.

O King, there shall never be for you any fear born of pestilence, nor shall you ever be separated from your own kinsmen. And while the auspicious sounds of drums resound, disease shall find no footing in your city. [The world] shall have the fatigue of its wandering dispelled by the showers of spray from the tears of the wives of your enemies.
Your fame, white as a row of elephant tusks, shall adorn even the three worlds.

(14.30cd) Then, having entrusted the wealth of your kingdom to your son and desiring to ascend the station marked by the emblem of Tārkṣya, you will become Manu, born from the Sun, the eighth among the lords of men in another birth. (14.31ab–14.31cd)
Having consecrated that lord of the earth with the nectar-like fluids of her speech, the daughter of the mountain departed for some place.
For the eyes of flesh are not capable of perceiving the path or the non-path of the great.
Then, when the tree of his own desire had borne fruit, the king did not fall under the sway of pride.
Even though he was great, he did not feel pride as others do during a festival; he did not falter there, nor did he sink into despondency.

(14.33cd) Then Suratha, his desires fulfilled, blazing with splendor like a second Indra, turned back toward the sage from whom all evil had departed—he who had been the very first guarantor of royal fortune. (14.34ab–cd)

The king, honoring with great respect the sons of the sages who were running toward him, eager to see his arrival, welcomed them with sincere blessings and by recounting the story of the grace bestowed upon him by the Daughter of the Mountain. Even the trees there, under the guise of their fresh blossoms, bore the beauty of horripilation arising from joy.

When the king had arrived, having perfected himself, they proclaimed his victory under the guise of the warbling of the black cuckoos. His progress announced by children who longed for the reward of reporting the arrival of their beloved,
that peerless man entered the dwellings of the sage with a body covered in horripilation born of joy.

Understanding the power of asceticism and knowing the sage’s resolve to engage in his natural duty, the wise sage, who was like a creator of sages, perceived the arrival of the king’s royal splendor even though it had not been announced. With head touching the ground, the sage approached in haste and raised up the king, whose lineage was noble.
And under the guise of his hands joined in salutation, with eyes filled with the tears of a woman in love, he offered an oblation of honor to the sinless one.
Having revealed his own state of having accomplished all that was to be done through words cooled by sacred learning— which betrayed his inner joy by the color of his face—
King Suratha, before the Sage, spoke again with his hands joined in excessive humility.
O Blessed One, my tongue is not able to utter your straightforwardness, which is beyond the range of words.

Yet this joy, sent forth by your grace, does not tolerate this person remaining silent. O sole benefactor of the world, even though you know that the praise of yourself is not desired, why indeed [is it offered]?

"I shall not do it, for I have no such desire; who would abandon their own welfare for the sake of another? (14.42cd) "Therefore, it is improper that you perceive in those like yourself an intention to perform service for the benefit of the world.
(14.43ab) "Does this sun cut away the most terrifying darkness only through the obstruction of others? (14.43cd)

Where even a son reveals his misconduct, where a beloved wife feels no shame, and where even friends turn away; O Vidura, when misfortune arises, it is you, with your grieving soul, who have acted for me as my father in that regard. My immersion in the triple-pathed river (the Gaṅgā) was without water, and this horse-sacrifice has become one devoid of ritual action.
"Since you were seen by me as if you yourself had personally assumed the form of the four-faced Brahmā seated upon his lotus throne,"—
to the king who was thus praising him, the master of those who speak little replied with haste:
"For such as he are not long inclined to listen to descriptions of their own deeds when they are recounted by others."
O King, by this nectar of your words, we have today been raised to the very pinnacle of bliss.
For the exaltation of the virtuous, who possess the lightning of wisdom, results in great benefit even for the entire world.
Though many may be capable of awakening others through the power of their intellect, it is those destined for greatness who truly bring about auspiciousness.
"O King, no one other than you is capable of performing this most difficult austerity again.
(14.48cd) A most excellent person considers even his own innate, unsurpassed virtue as a benefit bestowed by another who has rendered some small service.
(14.49ab) If brilliance were not inherent in gold by its very nature, then let it flash forth even in iron when purified by fire. (14.49cd)
Having thus addressed the god among men, the leader of the self-controlled once more dispatched many young brahmin students,
radiant in their antelope skins, to fetch the waters of the sacred fords with haste, desiring his consecration.
That treasury of compassion, having performed his consecration through the Sāman chants presided over by Varuṇa as the presiding deity—
She bestowed upon him a bride who followed the boon granted by the beloved of Hara, like a fresh blessing.
Those who had previously wronged him through their pseudo-ministers met their destruction in battle with one another;
for wealth born of unrighteousness not only perishes suddenly, but brings about the destruction of others as well.

Then, urged by other ministers who were devoted to valor and descended through hereditary succession, they sent forth secret agents to ascertain his whereabouts— agents who set out through every city, every forest, every plain, and every mountain. Having thoroughly learned from these hidden men that he, a portion of the Supreme Person, was residing in a hermitage, [they returned].

Bearing great joy and their armies, the ministers set out upon the road without delay. With the sharp sounds of the marching drums, as if proclaiming this festival born of the recovery of their lord throughout the quarters of the sky, they went swiftly; indeed, what longing do they not stir in those who are already full of joy?

Having bypassed even the smallest mountains and the camps of many kings fierce with rutting elephants, that army, as it marched toward him who was like the unfathomable ocean, found no place of rest anywhere.
For even one who speaks what is pleasant may become a source of affection; thus, under the guise of the mass of dust raised by the horses, [he spoke].
First the earth approached, as if wishing to announce the arrival of the beloved minister of the lord of the earth.
Hearing those roars of elephants accompanied by the sounds of excellent drums,
the herd of deer, with their restless eyes, followed after the courtyards of the forest huts and for a moment became agitated.
Before even the slightest doubt could arise in the heart of the king, the sage, as to what this might be, his spies announced:
"Victory! Victory, O Lord! Fortune has come to you.
Having established the royal camp along the river, his kinsmen took up residence there, their heat and fatigue dispelled by the forest.
Their fatigue from the road dispelled by the weight of their joy, those ministers quickly entered the hermitage.
Then the king, because his bow had long been set aside and thus lacked the dark calluses of the bowstring,
made his hand equal in size to that of the entire group of ministers as they bowed before him.

This king and these chief ministers, their eyes filled with tears of joy, only after a long time experienced the bliss of gazing upon one another’s lotus-like faces, even though it was already present before them. When his dear ministers had exchanged greetings of welfare and were seated on the honored seats, the monarch—

He proclaimed the power of the one who dwells in the lotus as if it were his own, and the affection of the ascetic as if he were his father. (14.63cd) When the news was reported by the multitude of messengers, even the young women from their respective fathers’ cities, lovely through their long-standing devotion, arrived there from their own homes. (14.64ab–cd)
Gazed upon gracefully by those slender women with eyes applied with fresh collyrium,
the king, whose ocean of passion had surged forth, embraced the god of love that had long been held in check.
Then, the venerable elder of the monarchs consecrated his own pure kingdom as a weighty sacrificial fee.

The seer, too, being gratified by his very service, bestowed upon him that [gift] along with a blessing. Whatever else the king desired was also granted before him; for adverse fate quickly shatters what is wished for, while a favorable one swiftly brings it about.

Bearing in his heart a deep anxiety arising from the thought that it would be so difficult to leave behind his dwelling with the noble family, the king, though eager to depart for the city, was unable to dismiss the sage immediately. (14.68) As those two—the king and the foremost of ascetics—stood there, their speech choked by tears rippling with the anticipation of their coming separation... (14.69)
The former asked for permission to depart, and the latter granted it with his head merely inclined.
Then, showing moisture in both his eyes and his heart toward these great seers— first this one and then the others—
he, bowing with devotion and grace that were free from partiality, placed the sacrificial fires upon his left side.
Then, having somehow turned back the young deer who were his forest friends and followed him out of devotion,

the universal monarch, resembling a blazing fire, set forth at an auspicious moment together with his ministers. By the sounds of his marching drums, which echoed through the caves of the great mountains with deep thundering, [the earth was shaken].
Even the seven horses, though wishing to bolt, were somehow brought to a standstill by the charioteer.
With the dust raised from the earth by the galloping multitude of steeds, which soiled the fame of his rival kings,
he traversed the elephants of the army in two or three days through the trees of the groves of his own city.

Having mounted his lofty elephant, like the sun of fierce radiance ascending the Eastern Mountain while displaying the glory of its rising, he entered the city preceded by his subjects; and at that moment, the joy of the citizens' arrival entered both the city and their hearts.
Thus ends the fourteenth canto, titled "The Attainment of the Kingdom," in the great poem named *Surathotsava*, composed by Śrī Someśvaradeva, the priest of the illustrious Gurjareśvara.
There is a place for the twice-born named Nagara, preeminent in its practice of virtuous conduct.
Kali can never cast a stain upon that city, which is purified by the three sacred fires (tretā).
How could there be any comparison between it and the world, which is frequented by gods and possesses excellent holy sites?

I bow to this Śrīnagara, whose splendor surpasses all other places; for even on its ground, which is a sole treasury of Vedic study and covered by the sacred texts, no child is seen in its palaces whose body is devoid of purity.

Where the Kali age— whose joy is unimpeded by the smoke from the fires of the sacrificial mouths that steal away the pleasure of the eyes, and by the Vedic recitations of throngs of students harsh to the ear—
finds no footing in the homes of the wise;

a place where darkness is shattered by the flickering flames of the five sacrificial fires, and where prosperity has been bestowed by the Three-Eyed Lord, whose flower-bow blazes with the fire of his own flame.
Beholding his supreme splendor and purity, the gods, finding even their residence in heaven tasteless, took up their dwelling under the pretext of being the Apsarases.
15.4cd We perpetually pay homage to that sage, the subduer of the senses, whose greatness was described by Kauśika as unbearable, while his own mind was repeatedly bewildered. 15.5ab
From Vasiṣṭha, whose conduct was pre-eminently unprecedented,
there emerged this great lineage, eminent for its virtuous deeds and established in the performance of sacrifices;
a lineage in which the Lord of All, with his hand adorned by the serpent-bracelet, is ever well-disposed.
They alone attain prosperity here in a family renowned by the name of Gula.
(15.6cd) In this stainless family, Śrī Solaśarman, the most eminent of the twice-born, obtained birth.
(15.7ab) He, at Prayāga, gratified the gods with soma juice in sacrifice and the ancestors with funeral cakes. (15.7cd)
"May he alone, as he descends gracefully upon the earth, be your bestower of prosperity"— thus remembering this boon of the Enemy of Smara (Śiva),
King Mūlarāja of Gurjara, having besieged him from afar, placed him before himself.
Just as the venerable Vasiṣṭha attained great preeminence in the lineage of the Sun.

By virtue of his own auspiciousness, he likewise performed the Vājapeya sacrifice according to the rules even in the Kali age within the lineage of the Caulukya kings. How much more could I possibly recount that collection of the wonders of his life?
A scholar of the Ṛgveda, a performer of a hundred sacrifices, a giver of gifts of food, and one who had conquered his senses—
when that lord of priests had passed away, Lallaśarman was then born in Aṅga;
he was the one who bestowed blessings upon the king named Cāmuṇḍarāja.
Endowed with both logical reasoning and majesty,
his son named Śrī Muñja became like the Self-born Creator himself upon the earth; for,
in order to attain the status of a Brahmin, he adopted a conduct among the virtuous that was like the girdle of muñja grass used at the investiture ceremony.
With such a family priest, born of a noble lineage and endowed with every virtue— like a bow made of excellent wood—
the King Durlabharāja believed there was nothing in the world that was unattainable for him.
His son, like the moon, brought peace to the world's afflictions, and like sandalwood, he provided cooling relief.
He who carries nectar and is marked by the moon attained true sovereignty over the twice-born.
By King Bhīma, whose rise was brought about by his blessings,
that fame was made manifest— white with rice grains washed in milk.
By him, through that [ascetic practice] capable of reaching the state beyond desire, all these various manifestations of the Lord were rendered white even without the smearing of ashes.
(15.16cd) When his father had departed there after piercing the sun, the illustrious son Āmaśarman came into being. (15.17ab)

Having performed seven sacrifices with all their constituent parts, he who was free from desire attained the title of "Emperor" (samrāj). At all times, his ears were filled with blessings; that king named Śrīkarṇa made the circle of the earth, bounded by the oceans, such that the tears from the eyes of the wives of his enemies were shed.

By him, whose appearance was emulated by the sages, those gifts, those dwellings, and those lakes as beautiful as rows of lotuses were created with the wealth bestowed by the kings born of the Cūlukya lineage. Having surveyed his entire kingdom, the royal priest of the Lord of Dhārā [performed these deeds].
A *kṛtyā* was reportedly conjured for the purpose of destroying him, who had troubled the Caulukya dynasty;
but while he was performing austerities with mantras, she was repelled by them, and having destroyed that very sorcerer right there, she vanished quickly like a flash of lightning from a tree.
Therefore, the prince, whose form was delicate, arose like an embodied mass of ascetic merit.
A voice that grants the rise of one's own royal kingdom dwelt in his mouth as if it were the personified Power (Śakti).
Even the Lord of the Sindhu earth, though possessed of exceedingly mature majesty, was bound by him.
Even the Lord of Mālava, though possessed of vast forces, was led captive along with his wife;

and even that proud King of the Sapādalakṣa was taught the lesson of prostrating at [his] feet by the illustrious King Siddha. Such is this entire majesty which belongs to the blessings of him [the Lord].

He who served as the domestic priest to a universal monarch performed sacrifices adorned with *kuśa* grass and constructed more than a hundred reservoirs; having seen both the visible and the unseen fruits of such merit, he departed for the third heaven, as if out of longing for the status of a priest to a king whose charioteer was *Ṛju*.
Sarvadeva acquired the entire essence of the legal codes (smṛti) composed by King Manu, the son of the Sun;
he performed the proper worship of Viṣṇu at sacrifices and triumphed over the Lord of the Gods (Indra) in those very rites.
He made men—who were ignorant of other paths—men who had achieved their life's purpose.

When that best of kṣatriyas, worthy of homage, had entered the path of the funeral flames, the Vedic rite was subsequently performed for him by his son, named Āmiga. For that man, who delighted in the performance of virtuous deeds, these two things became a source of shame: [the fact that he had not himself performed the rites, and that they were now being performed by another].
Hearing one's own praises from superiors and remaining within the prison of cyclic existence (saṃsāra)—[these are the faults].

15.27cd The eldest, the most excellent among all the learned, named Śrī Sarvadeva; and the illustrious younger brother, Kumāra, who has cast away the darkness that is difficult to overcome through the wealth of spiritual welfare (śreyas). 15.28ab

Then Muñja, that elephant among the twice-born, and his younger brother Ahaḍa, who was not dull-witted regarding the path of justice— these four sons were born from him like the four Vedas from Brahmā.
Having cast the limbs of Kumārapāla, the lord of the Cālukyas, into the waters of the Gaṅgā...
By Śrī Sarvadeva, the Brahmins of Gayā and Prayāga were rendered fulfilled through his gifts.
In every place there were tanks, and day after day, the worship of Śiva was performed; honor was shown to every single Brahmin, and praise resounded in every house. (15.29cd–15.30)
Even though he was obstructed by King Kumārapāla’s son, who seized the sun while it was eclipsed by Rāhu, the priest did not accept his heap of jewels. He,
who was skilled in purity and self-restraint, had propitiated the one known as Kaṭukeśvara— the half-body joined with the Daughter of the Mountain.

He removed from King Ajayapāla that terrible agony born from the multitude of wounds sustained on the field of battle. 15.32cd Beholding the world reduced to mere skeletons by the power of a calamitous age, he—filled with exceptional indignation—caused the illustrious Mūlarāja, who had crushed the kings of his enemies, to effect the release of those [prisoners]. 15.33ab–cd

He who was made a peerless king by Pratāpamalla— the lord of all preeminent men, whose lineage was fierce in the slaughter of ten million wicked enemies, and who was a thorn to the Kauṅkaṇas on the field of battle—
was appointed as the commander-in-chief, known as Kumāra, by that moon of the Cālukyas. (15.34)
Then, having swiftly conquered the rival kings with irresistible force,
he himself bestowed upon that king— the object of his sacrifice— the desired prosperity of that realm, like a blessing, through the syllables formed by the ranks of his own heroic warriors.
When Vindhyavarman, the lord of Dhārā, had departed after abandoning the battle— though he was swelling with unfailing wrath—
he [the king] plundered his city of Gogasthāna, where he even dug a well in place of a palace; furthermore,
being enraged, he seized base metals from the territory of the Lord of Mālava.
Furthermore, that which was given as a śrāddha at Gayā by him who, being free from anger,

[conquered] the invincible; having defeated the incomparable force of the Mleccha lord, the queen, near the lake of the celestial river, duly offered libations with its waters for the satisfaction of her ancestors.
Now, having spent a year on the surface of the earth in pursuit of liberation,
he who was wise performed [these deeds] for the sake of the king, for his own sake, and for the sake of the subjects;
he who expands the sixfold duties and the three worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ.
He whose fame and stainless luster never forsake him; from whom the display of weapons arises both in sacrifice and in battle, and from whom praise is uplifted;
he in whose heart the thread of the Veda and the sovereignty of a kingdom throb incessantly. (15.39)
Like Arundhatī to her beloved husband, she was his command, Arundhatī by name;
she was like Lakṣmī herself on earth, Lakṣmī in appearance.
His first-born son, a temple of tranquility, was Mahādeva by name.
Sarasvatī herself is most highly pleased by that which is placed in his hand, as if by mud.
This younger brother of this lord of the earth, named Someśvaradeva, was born as his junior sibling; he was Vijaya, of renowned lineage.
Through those three— low, middle, and high— established in their respective positions as men,
his lineage became highly honored throughout the world, like the science of grammar;
having perceived the world-filling abundance of virtues in the poet Someśvaradeva.
Thus it has been stated by Hari, Hara, Subhaṭa, and other preeminent poets:
"In the case of the poet Śrī Someśvaradeva and the sun, even when [the former] has discarded the consumption of grass, [his poetry] still bestows aesthetic flavor. 15.44cd–15.45cd.
The eloquent speech of the poet Somaśarman,
who is like the springtime of the Goddess of Speech and an ocean of literary art, shakes the wise with its nectar.
Your face is a hundred-petaled lotus, possessed of excellent color and filled with all the sciences.
May the Goddess of Speech protect her own book as if it were Someśvaradeva’s work.
(15.47cd) In this world, there is a drum proclaiming that the station of Vasiṣṭha is the ultimate goal; yet even among these [descendants], Munja and others were born who were preeminent. (15.48ab)
Born into another family, he was further made a son by the daughter of Śatadhṛti, whose heart was gladdened by his ninefold poetic virtues.
By means of his poetry, which is the locus of the flavor of refined new words, and by a drama composed in just half a watch of the night— || 15.48cd–15.49ab ||
He brought the members of the assembly in the court of the illustrious King Bhīma under the sway of immense joy;
for even those who cherish the status of the lords of poets feel pain in their ears when his speech, harsh as a saw, is proclaimed.
Yet, a poet such as you is rarely seen again on this earth—
he who, with his well-spoken verses, seems to perform a consecration with nectar. One is dull in prosody, another is deficient in grammar, while yet another is merely skilled in ornamentation.
In the matter of meaning, there is some futile exertion; on the path to the treasure of eloquence, he is some blind man.
Yet, alone among those who compete with the sweet sound of the anklets of the Daughter of Brahmā as she sports within the mouth [of Śiva], the son of Kumāra composes poetry.
Now that the illustrious Hemacandra—who has taken refuge in scholarship that is otherwise without support—has gone to heaven...
Seeing that these two— the cessation of his vow to benefit the world and the absence of the illustrious Prahlādana— resided here in the crown-jewel of ministers, the illustrious Vastupāla,
the poet commenced this outpouring of joy under the guise of praising his fame.
In the ocean of the Prāgvāṭa lineage, there was formerly Śrī Caṇḍapa, like the moon;
from him was born Caṇḍaprasāda, an abode of wonderful truth and purity. His son was Soma, whose intellect was radiant with statesmanship, and his son was Aśvarāja.
Then Śrī Vastupāla, whose soul was purified, who was born from that [minister’s] body, and who was born of merit, came into being.
His fame rivaled the blossoming *mallī* jasmine; he was Śrī Malladeva, the elder brother. And his younger brother, named Tejaḥpāla, became the preeminent minister.
May the illustrious Vastupāla live long— he who always bestows illumination upon the quarters with his glories,
which are as bright as the teeth of Kerala women adorned with camphor;
and for embodied beings whose vision has failed, the divine goddess Kālīśvarī is the medicine.
In this body, which is a canvas for manifold wonders, the Lord Śrī Vaidyanātha is the refuge;
in the heart worn out by the fever of worldly existence, Viṣṇu is ever present for the sake of joy;
and when poverty is sought to be destroyed, this Śrī Vastupāla is the goal.

He does not speak harsh words even in anger, nor does he touch the vital parts of another even in jest. This wise moon of honor ceases from pride; and when besought by those in need, he never desists from giving. He bestows wealth—attained through the toil of incessant service to the lords of the earth—even without effort.
Furthermore, that very person who reflects upon a matter for the benefit of others is a true *vastupāla* (protector of things).
I speak the truth; let there be no offense here, even though I have become excessively harsh by nature.
This minister has been tested in both favorable and adverse circumstances, and nothing wicked has been observed in his virtuous conduct.
May this minister be blessed—he whose conduct is attended by a circle of subjects whose lives have been elevated by his daily acts of charity.
By the spreading rays of his fame, which are equal to the moon, the nights have become like the full moon of the Rākā phase.
Other officials obtain curses from the people for their sins.
This minister, moreover, governs by means of repeated acts of overbearing authority.
(15.61cd) Indeed, those very men are praised by the cattle-like kings as being wise, from whom the subjects immediately fall into ruin. (15.62ab)
Thus, for the virtuous who dwell somewhere in constant trepidation due to their secure state, you alone are now the minister who bestows the welfare of Śiva upon the earth.
O you who are humble with modesty, without you—who have shattered the miserable condition of supplicants by the granting of wealth—[the world would be lost]. 15.62cd–15.63ab.
O Vastupāla, no one in this world can wipe away the ill-omened inscription upon the skull of the virtuous.
O illustrious Vastupāla, your extraordinary life-story shines forth here in this palace, which is smeared with the liquid of cow-dung and whitened by the nectar of your fame. (15.63cd–15.64)
She is saluted by nectars, offered to by snows, propitiated by stars,
honored by the waves of the Gaṅgā, familiarized by the rays from the tusks of the elephants of the quarters,
cultivated with camphor, embraced by sandalwood pastes, and adorned [by them all].

While this sacrificial session of poetry was underway, the family priest of the gods of Gurjara, having thus honored the worthy recipient— the minister—
considered himself to have achieved his purpose.
This poem concerning the Mother of the Prince— that sole goddess of the world— was composed by that son of the prince,
who was an expert in the Vedas, the Smṛtis, grammar, and the science of sacrifice.
Thus ends the fifteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Poet’s Praise," in the great poem named *Surathotsava*, composed by Śrī Someśvaradeva, the priest of the illustrious Gurjareśvara.
